To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the personality and learning style of medical students predict their attitudes towards work and their satisfaction with their work and with medicine as a profession.

approaches to work and learning style in doctors are stable over time, and are associated with personality traits, and are associated, in turn, with doctors' stress, burnout, and attitudes to medicine as a career.

approaches to work and perceptions of the workplace climate of doctors are predicted by personality and learning styles, which are stable over time, and that these factors in turn predict stress, burnout, and satisfaction with medicine, which are also partly predicted by personality.
In summary, our research is concerned with
doctors' approaches to learning and work and how these relate to personality.

the extent to which the personality and learning style of doctors predicts how they approach their work, how they perceive their working environment, and how this affects their levels of stress, burn-out and satisfaction with their career.
the extent to which the attitudes and behaviours of doctors, and the way in which doctors perceive their workplace, can be explained in terms of personality and learning styles.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the personality traits of doctors are more important than their learning styles in influencing their approach to work and their attitudes to medicine.

doctors' attitudes to their work and their workplace, and their satisfaction with medicine as their career, are predicted by their personality and learning style, both at the time of applying to medical school and as final year medical students, but that the workplace climate itself is also important.

personality, learning style, approaches to work, perceived work climate and stress, burnout, and satisfaction with work in medicine are all interrelated, and that all these factors are determined by personality.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
personality, approaches to work, and learning styles all contribute to doctors' attitudes to their work, and that these attitudes, in turn, influence their stress, burnout, and satisfaction.
personality and learning style are important in predicting how doctors will approach their work, their perceptions of the work climate, their stress, burnout, and satisfaction with their careers.

doctors with a deep approach to study and learning, who are conscientious, open and agreeable, and who have a deep approach to their work, are more satisfied with medicine as a profession and have lower stress and burnout scores than other doctors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the attitudes of doctors to work, their stress levels, burnout, and satisfaction with medicine can be predicted by measures of personality taken years before.
doctors with a preference for deep learning and an internal locus of control have a more positive attitude to work and to their career.
doctors' attitudes to their work and their work environment are not determined by their work experience, but by their personalities and their approaches to learning.
